references.text: John the Baptist repeats the same testimony: "I am not the Messiah, but I have been sent ahead of him" (Jn 3:28). This is a direct parallel to his confession that he is not the Christ.

The people wondered if John might be the Messiah, but he denied it and pointed further to the one who was stronger than him (Lk 3:15–16). John's humble attitude confirms his role as the forerunner, not as the Messiah.
Paul quotes John the Baptist's own testimony: "I am not the one you think I am" (Acts 13:25). This shows that John's denial of being the Christ was well known in the early church.
The Pharisees then ask who John is, and he points to the one coming after him, for whom he is not worthy to untie the sandal strap (Jn 1:25–27). This is the immediate follow-up to his confession.

Also in Matthew, John the Baptist emphasizes the difference between himself and the coming Messiah: He baptizes with water, but the one who comes after him will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (Mt 3:11–12).

While John the Baptist refuses to take the title Messiah, Peter confesses the opposite about Jesus: "You are the Messiah" (Mk 8:29). These two confessions complement each other – one rejects the title for himself, while the other attributes it to Jesus.
John was not the light, but came to testify about the light (Jn 1:8). His role was to point away from himself and toward Christ, which his open confession of not being the Messiah confirms.
